prompt: Explain what a locally running Large Language Model (LLM) is. Clarify the difference between local inference and local training. Explain why a model trained in the cloud can still be run locally after downloading its weights. Give a simple example.

Explain the main stages of an LLM lifecycle: pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, alignment, quantization, inference, and deployment. Describe what each stage does and clarify which stages are optional for someone who only wants to run an existing model locally.
Explain the difference between a base language model and an instruction-tuned model. Describe how their expected behavior differs and give examples of when a developer might choose each.

Explain how RAM, VRAM, model parameter count, numerical precision, and context length affect local LLM inference. Distinguish model-weight memory from total runtime memory. Avoid presenting hardware estimates as universal guarantees.

A computer has 8 GB system RAM and no dedicated GPU. Explain what factors determine whether it can run a small quantized language model. Discuss CPU inference, available memory, model size, context length, and performance trade-offs. Do not guarantee that a particular model will run without knowing the operating system and available memory.

Compare CPU inference, NVIDIA CUDA GPU inference, and Apple Silicon inference for local LLMs. Explain memory considerations, software compatibility, performance trade-offs, and why benchmark results depend on the model and hardware.

Explain the difference between Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp. Describe their typical use cases, user experience, model support, and how they relate to running models locally. Avoid claiming that one tool is universally best.

Explain what a model context window is. Describe how input tokens, conversation history, system instructions, and generated output use context capacity. Explain why a larger context window can increase memory requirements.

Explain temperature, top-k, and top-p sampling in LLM text generation. Describe how each influences token selection and response variability. Include practical guidance without suggesting that one setting guarantees factual accuracy.

Explain FP32, FP16, INT8, and 4-bit representations in the context of storing LLM weights. Compare their raw storage requirements relative to FP32, and clarify that actual runtime memory also includes metadata, activations, context cache, and implementation overhead. Avoid treating FP16 and integer quantization as identical techniques.

Explain post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT). Describe their differences, whether retraining is generally required, the role of calibration data in some PTQ methods, and the potential quality trade-offs.

Explain the GGUF model format and its relationship to llama.cpp. Describe why GGUF files are commonly used for local inference, what quantization labels such as Q4_K_M and Q8_0 indicate at a high level, and why file size alone does not determine inference speed or quality.

Explain the difference between full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA for adapting an existing LLM. Describe which parameters are updated, the role of adapters, memory trade-offs, and situations where each approach may be appropriate.

Explain supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for an instruction-following language model. Describe the structure of instruction-response training examples, dataset preparation, training, validation, and common risks such as duplicates, poor labels, and data leakage.

Explain knowledge distillation for language models using the teacher-student approach. Describe the teacher model, student model, training dataset, and learning objective. Explain why a smaller student may be cheaper to run but is not guaranteed to match the teacher's capabilities.

Compare response-based, logit-based, feature-based, and relation-based knowledge distillation for LLMs. Explain what information each method uses and distinguish ordinary supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated answers from directly matching teacher logits.

Describe a practical black-box, response-based LLM distillation workflow when the teacher is accessible only through a text-generation API. Cover prompt design, response generation, dataset validation, student fine-tuning, held-out evaluation, and teacher/student licensing considerations. Clarify that teacher logits are unavailable in this setup unless explicitly exposed.

Write a Python 3.12 function named is_prime(n) that returns True if an integer is prime and False otherwise. Handle negative integers, zero, one, two, and even numbers correctly. Include type hints, a short explanation, and example calls. Reject booleans and non-integer inputs with TypeError.

Write a Python 3.12 program that reads a JSONL file containing instruction-response records and validates that each non-empty line is a JSON object with non-empty string fields named id, prompt, and response. Report line numbers for invalid records. Use only the Python standard library and include an example input and usage.

Design an evaluation plan for a student LLM distilled from a teacher model. Explain how to create a held-out test set, compare teacher and student responses, evaluate factual correctness and task performance, measure latency and memory use, and identify overfitting. Distinguish automated metrics from human review and do not assume that similarity to the teacher always means correctness.
